opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting questions right now, and honestly I see them as two quite different paths that people sometimes blur together.

When I say "language game," I'm borrowing a bit from Wittgenstein: meaning comes from how words are used inside a shared system of rules and conventions. Large language models are extraordinarily good at playing that game. They've absorbed how humans talk about the world, the patterns and associations, the way one sentence tends to follow another. And because human language encodes so much of our accumulated knowledge, playing the game well can look a lot like understanding. In many practical cases it's useful enough that the distinction doesn't seem to matter.

But I think language is a compressed, lossy, very human-centric projection of reality. It's a communication protocol, not the world itself. A lot of what we know, like how a cup falls off a table, how to move through a crowded room, how light changes when you turn your head, isn't really stored in language. Babies and animals have rich models of the physical world long before, or entirely without, language. So if you only play the language game, you're learning the shadows on the cave wall, to use another old metaphor. You get the structure of descriptions, not necessarily the structure of the thing being described.

A world model, to me, is a system that has an internal representation of how the world works: its state, its dynamics, cause and effect, so it can predict, imagine, and plan. That has to be grounded in something richer than text: vision, video, interaction, maybe embodiment. That's part of why I've spent so much of my career on visual representation learning. I think vision is a much higher-bandwidth window into reality, and it doesn't come pre-digested by humans the way language does.

That said, I don't think it's an either-or. Language is incredibly powerful as an interface and as a scaffold for abstraction and reasoning. The ideal system probably has a grounded world model at its core, with language sitting on top as a way to communicate, query, and reason symbolically. What worries me a little is the current tendency to treat language as the foundation and bolt vision on as an "adapter," as if seeing were just another tokenizer. I suspect that ordering is backwards. If we want intelligence that truly understands and acts in the physical world, we need to take the world itself seriously as the training signal, not just humanity's commentary about it.

So my short answer: the language game is a remarkable achievement, but it isn't the destination. The world model is the harder, deeper problem, and I think that's where a lot of the next decade of research needs to go.

r001.rationale: The response says meaning comes from how words are used within shared rules and conventions, expressing that meaning is determined by use in shared practices.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've been thinking about a lot, actually, because I come at it from the vision side, and for years we were kind of in the shadow of what language models were doing.

Here's how I'd frame it. Wittgenstein's idea of a language game is that meaning comes from use. Words don't point at things in the world in some fixed, one-to-one way; they get their meaning from how people play with them inside shared practices. And when I look at what large language models have done, that's exactly what they've learned. They've absorbed an enormous amount of human language use, and from that they've extracted something that looks like understanding. It's a very powerful compression of how humans talk about the world.

But notice what's missing. The language game is already a game played by beings who have bodies, who see, who move, who bump into things. The text on the internet is the residue of that. It's the shadow on the wall. So a language model learns the rules of the game without ever having played the underlying game of being in the world. It knows that a cup falls if you knock it off a table, because people have written that sentence, but it has never seen a cup fall.

That's where I think world models come in. A world model, to me, is not about describing the world in language. It's about internalizing the structure of the world itself: space, time, physics, how things persist and change when you look away from them. Humans and animals have this long before they have language. A baby has a world model at a few months old, and it has no words at all. Language gets layered on top of that.

So the relationship I'd propose is that language is an interface, and the world model is the substrate. Language is how we communicate about the world, align with each other, pass down knowledge. It's incredibly efficient as a protocol. But it's lossy, and it presupposes that both sides already share a grounding in reality. If you only have the protocol, you get something that sounds right but can be brittle in surprising ways.

What's interesting in the current moment is that these two directions are starting to meet. On one side you have language models trying to reach down into perception and action, through multimodal training and agents. On the other side you have people like me working on vision and generative models, trying to build systems that learn how the visual world evolves, and then realizing that at some point you want language on top so you can steer them and reason with them.

I don't think one replaces the other. My honest view is that we've gotten the order a bit backwards relative to how nature did it. We built the language layer first because the data was there and it was cheap. Now we're going back and trying to build the foundation under it. And the hard question, the one I don't have a clean answer to, is whether a world model learned mostly from passive video and images is enough, or whether you really need interaction, you need to act in the world and see the consequences, to get the kind of grounding that makes the language game actually mean something.

r001.rationale: The response says meaning comes from use and that words get their meaning from how people use them within shared practices.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that language gets its meaning through use, and that use happens in a world. When we talk about language games, we’re talking about more than arranging words correctly. We’re talking about what someone is trying to do with those words, what context they’re in, and what counts as a successful response.

A world model can help support that. If I say, “Can you open the window?” you understand that I’m probably making a request, rather than asking you to assess your physical abilities. That understanding involves language conventions, but also some model of the situation: there’s a window, it can be opened, and opening it may change the temperature in the room.

For AI, the interesting question is how much of that understanding can be learned from language alone. Language contains a tremendous amount of information about the world, so I wouldn’t draw a hard boundary between language learning and world modeling. But describing an action and understanding its consequences through observation and interaction provide different kinds of evidence.

So I see them as complementary. Language games give us a way to participate in shared activities; world models help us anticipate what will happen as we participate. The challenge is connecting linguistic competence with an understanding that remains useful when the situation changes.

r001.rationale: The response says language gets meaning through use in the world and explains that language games involve what people do with words in shared activities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the relationship depends on what we mean by a world model. If we mean an internal representation that lets a system predict what will happen and how its actions will affect the environment, then language can express part of that model. But being good at language doesn’t automatically tell us how much of the world a system understands.

Language games are interesting because meaning depends on use. The same sentence can be a description, a joke, a warning, or an instruction. To respond appropriately, you need some understanding of the situation: who is speaking, what they want, and what consequences a response might have. So participating in language games can require something like a model of the social world.

At the same time, language gives you a very particular view of reality. People describe things that are worth communicating, and leave enormous amounts of ordinary physical experience unstated. You rarely explain every detail of how an object moves when you push it. That makes me cautious about equating learning from language with learning everything needed for a world model.

The question I find useful is: can the system use what it has learned to predict and act in a new situation? Can it connect a verbal description to what it sees, update its understanding when something unexpected happens, and anticipate the consequences of an action? Language is a powerful resource for building that ability, but perception and interaction give us additional ways to develop it—and to test whether it is actually there.

r001.rationale: The response says meaning depends on use and context, but does not clearly state that language-game meaning is determined by actions within worldly practices.
